bio.en: Oji Udezue is Chief Product Officer at Typeform and a veteran product and growth leader who has built and scaled products at Microsoft, Atlassian, Calendly, and Twitter.
bio.zh: Oji Udezue 是 Typeform 的首席产品官（CPO），也是一位资深的产品与增长领袖，曾在 Microsoft、Atlassian、Calendly 和 Twitter 打造并扩展产品。

summary.en: Oji presents frameworks for finding big B2B SaaS ideas by targeting high-frequency, broad workflows, and introduces the 'zone of benefit' concept that a solution must be roughly 3x better than the status quo to win. He discusses how to identify your ideal customer profile and how companies can navigate from low-frequency niches toward category-leading positions. The conversation draws on his rare cross-company perspective on what actually drives product and growth.
summary.zh: Oji 提出了一套寻找大型 B2B SaaS 创意的框架——瞄准高频、广覆盖的工作流，并引入了“收益区间（zone of benefit）”的概念：解决方案必须比现状好大约 3 倍才能取胜。他讨论了如何识别理想客户画像（ICP），以及企业如何从低频小众定位逐步迈向品类领先。对话依托他在多家不同公司的罕见跨视角，剖析了究竟是什么真正驱动产品与增长。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Products who try to be viral just for what I call synthetic virality that fail. Because in the end, if you're synthetically viral and people get to the product and it sucks, that's it. Slack wasn't even viral, there was no synthetic virality. Slack couldn't even connect to organizations for the longest time. You could be working on the third floor, and someone using Slack on the fourth floor and you would have no clue, there's no way to share it with them. But what happens when you went to lunch? People are like, "We got Slack and this is amazing." And people on the third floor are like, "Holy shit, when can we get it?" Boom, boom, boom. This is the bedrock of virality. Build a great product that solves a sharp problem.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Okay, so I want to start with frameworks. You've written and shared a bunch of really interesting frameworks for how to think about product and growth, and so I just want to dig into a couple of them. And one of them is around how to find big B2B SaaS ideas and it's around finding the right workflow. Could you just share this framework and also just how founders and also investors can use this idea to find big ideas?
turns.zh: 我很乐意。首先我想谈谈框架。你曾撰写并分享过许多关于产品与增长思考的有趣框架，我想深入探讨其中几个。其中一个是如何挖掘B2B SaaS领域的重大创意，关键在于找到合适的工作流程。你能否分享这个框架，并讲讲创始人和投资者如何借助这一思路寻找突破性创意？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Thank you. So I think you're referring to where do you fish to find a unicorn.
turns.zh: 谢谢。您指的应该是如何寻找独角兽企业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's it.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: And the thing behind that is people can find that on Substack and the Medium, my writings. But the premise is that there's a lot of risk in building startups, and the last decade of product management and startups has really focused on the method of building software and companies. We talk about the lean approach, we talk about fail fast, [inaudible 00:04:28] and so on and so forth. And I think that that was a necessary phase for us because a lot of innovation was just the ideas of founders unvalidated by customers, and we needed this inflection point in our discipline. People need to understand though that customer science is not the solution to everything otherwise OpenAI will never have done anything. It's also innovation. And so the problem space and the solutions to the problems space is still a big driver of success in building software companies. (00:05:03): What problem are you really solving? And if you believe that the problem space is key, so what problems will predict success? In B2B SaaS especially, which is much easier to circumscribe is where I start to think about, look, how do you tell from the beginning? Because an investor as well as an operator. Now to segment this space, I think of two dimensions. One is how many departments in the company does the workflow you're trying to solve apply to? Is it just a few or is it all of them? And the second is how intense or how frequent is the workflow executed? Is it daily? Is it weekly? Is it three times a week? And so on and so forth. Now if you draw a nice quadrant of these two things, then you can start to have some predictive power. Things that are useful in every department I call every one workflows, like things like collaboration, like Slack, email, calendaring, workflows, social knowledge and Notion and so on and so forth. (00:06:04): And then things that apply to single departments, I call niche and that's what I call niche. And then the intensity is about frequency. A month is not infrequent, daily is super frequent. If you divide the market or the enterprise into frequency and into how broad the workflow is, you can actually have predictive power. And what I found by looking at the biggest company is public and private in each quadrant was that every one frequent workflows intuitively are the most profitable to work on, but also the hardest to get into because they're dominated by Microsoft and Google and very, very large companies. For example, one of my friends is the CEO of Coda. And so this is interesting, because he's in that space, for him to think about. (00:06:58): And then the place where B2B SaaS really thrives is niche workflows that are highly frequent. High ni is what I call it, high frequency niche. And then there are the other two quadrants that are a bit more challenging. And then you have to figure out how to navigate your way into one of the other two. If you are in one of the top two quadrants, high ni and high everyone and you solve a really important problem, workflow problem, you can probably turn into a billion-dollar company. If you do the other two, there's some challenges that you have to go through. And the framework talks about how you should navigate those places into success. And I think it's very important because if this is true, and by the way, like I said, I did some validation on it, founders can start to, before they invest years, start to think about what probability of success is. And if you're an investor like me or VC, you can start to think about how you deploy your money.
turns.zh:
背后的原因在于，人们可以在Substack和Medium上找到我的文章。但前提是，创业公司面临诸多风险，过去十年的产品管理和创业实践主要聚焦于软件和公司构建的方法论。我们谈论精益方法、快速迭代等理念，我认为这对我们来说是一个必要的阶段，因为当时许多创新仅是创始人未经客户验证的想法，我们需要这个行业变革的契机。不过人们需要明白，客户科学并非万能良药，否则OpenAI永远不会取得任何成果。创新本身也是解决问题的重要手段。因此，问题空间与解决方案的匹配度仍是软件公司成功的核心驱动力。（00:05:03）：你真正在解决什么问题？如果你认为问题空间是关键，那么哪些问题能预示成功？尤其在B2B SaaS领域，界定更清晰的领域让我开始思考：如何从一开始就能判断？作为投资者和运营者，我认为可以从两个维度入手：一是所要解决的工作流适用于公司多少部门？是少数部门还是全部部门？二是工作流的执行频率和强度如何？是每日执行？每周执行？还是每周三次？如此等等。将这两个维度绘制成二维坐标图，就能获得一定的预测能力。适用于每个部门的工作流，我称之为通用工作流，例如协作工具Slack、邮件、日历、Notion等。

（00:06:04）：而适用于单个部门的工具，我称之为利基产品。这里的“利基”指的是专注某个细分领域。至于执行频率，月度执行不算罕见，日执行则极为频繁。如果将市场或企业按执行频率和工作流覆盖范围划分，就能获得预测能力。通过观察各个象限中的头部公私企业，我发现高频、广覆盖的工作流通常最易盈利，但进入门槛也最高，往往由微软、谷歌等巨头把持。例如，我的朋友Coda的CEO就深有体会。

（00:06:58）：B2B SaaS真正蓬勃发展的领域在于高频利基工作流。这里的“高频利基”指的是高频、高覆盖的利基产品。其他两个象限则更具挑战性。企业需找到切入点。如果处于高频、高覆盖的象限，并解决关键工作流问题，或许能成长为十亿美元级公司；若处于其他象限，则需克服重重难关。框架旨在指导如何在这些领域取得成功，这点至关重要。若这一观点成立（我已验证过），那么创始人就能在投入多年前评估成功概率，投资者也能更明智地配置资金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are examples of companies in each of those quadrants? If you can frame this and I don't know if you have this in your head already.
turns.zh: 每个象限中的公司都有哪些例子？如果你能把这个框架整理出来，我不知道你是否已经在脑海中有了答案。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: High frequency everyone workflows tend to be things that are done by the doorman to the CEO. So it's email, it's collaboration, it is writing, it is math, all the basic things. At Atlassian, we spend a lot of time thinking about this. So Word, we've had word processing forever in the workspace. Things like Notion and Confluence are huge as sort of evolution of that, Slack, email. Companies in that space, Google, Microsoft, Atlassian, et cetera. And the high ni, which is high frequency niche, you have things like Jira, you have things like tools for recruiters, you have martech, you have sales tech. (00:08:49): And we know the companies behind them, Atlassian, Salesforce, so on and so forth. And then in the low frequency everyone, you have things like maybe form tools. And actually, they're not that many of them, low frequency everyone or even expense. Actually, the best expensing. Not everyone does it all the time, but everyone essentially has to do some of it, mostly, at least a lot of people. And then there's a low frequency niche, which is particular department. So planning, which is done by FPNA, but done infrequently, things like that.
turns.zh: 高频日常工作流程通常是从门卫到CEO都要用到的东西。比如邮件、协作、写作、数学等基础功能。在Atlassian，我们花了很多时间思考这个问题。Word在工作场所已经存在很久了。Notion和Confluence等工具是其进化版本，还有Slack、邮件等。属于这个领域的公司有谷歌、微软、Atlassian等。高频利基市场方面，Jira之类的工具，还有招聘工具、营销技术、销售技术等。（00:08:49）我们知道这些背后的公司，比如Atlassian、Salesforce等等。然后在低频日常工作流程中，可能有表单工具之类的。实际上这类产品并不多，要么是低频日常，要么是费用管理。实际上，最好的费用管理工具不是每个人都会一直使用，但基本上每个人至少偶尔会用到。还有低频利基市场，针对特定部门。比如规划，由FPNA负责，但使用频率较低。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How frequent is frequent in your experience? Does it have to be once a week at least? What do you think is that minimum bar?
turns.zh: 在你的经验中，“频繁”到底有多频繁？至少每周一次吗？你认为最低标准是什么？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Frequent is every day really or multiple times a week. Infrequent starts to be like two times a week, once a month. And of course there's a big interregnum in the middle of that.
turns.zh: 频繁指的是每天使用，或者每周多次使用。低频则可能是每周两次、每月一次。当然，两者之间还有很大的过渡空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that there are examples of companies that succeeded in those lower quadrants of infrequent, say the expensing use case. Do you have a sense of what it takes to win there? Because I imagine most startups are in that area, and I imagine founders are like, what can we do to win still?
turns.zh: 有趣的是，在低频日常工作流程领域也有成功的公司案例，比如费用管理场景。你觉得在那里获胜需要什么条件？因为我猜大多数初创公司都在这个领域，创始人可能会问，我们该怎么做才能在那里胜出？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Well, this isn't a static framework in the sense that companies are not destined to be one of these things. The essence of strategy is to navigate from the curve of travel is essentially go from the lower to the higher. Atlassian is trying to go from high niche to high everyone with Confluence and with all the tools that they have. People below are trying to get into the high frequency niche by focusing on their core customer. So what it looks like in say low frequency everyone workflows, something like that is, well, if some people are using it infrequently, but they must use it, well that's a good thing. But then maybe you provide a module that is used by the finance department every day, and so suddenly you're moving into the high frequency everyone workflow. So it's about finding a part of the organization that considers this mission-critical and then solving their problems beyond the problems for everyone for example, in that quadrant.
turns.zh: 嗯，这不是一个静态的框架，公司不一定非得局限于这些类别。战略的本质是从曲线中找到出路，基本上是从低到高过渡。Atlassian正试图通过Confluence和现有工具从高利基市场转向高频日常市场。低端市场的公司则试图通过专注核心客户进入高频日常市场。比如说，如果有些人偶尔使用某个工具，但又必须使用，那就是件好事。但也许你提供了一个财务部门每天使用的模块，这样一来你就进入了高频日常工作流程。因此，关键在于找到一个认为这项任务至关重要的部门，然后解决他们的问题，超越普通用户的需求，例如在那个象限中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that comes to mind of either at Calendly or Typeform or Atlassian where you pushed it further up the frequency direction or the everyone direction?
turns.zh: 在Calendly、Typeform或Atlassian中，有没有例子能让你想到他们把频率或覆盖面提升到了更高的水平？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: For example, at Typeform, now this is real for me, Typeform technically is low frequency niche or low frequency everyone, depending on how easy it is to use and how it surrounds the customer. And one of the things that I'm trying to do as part of product strategy is to move it into high frequency niche, high ni, which is a very productive place to be. So for marketers, for salespeople, I want to make sure that they think of us first. And because we are particularly good at customer facing interactions, if they think that we are the way to win new business and to make money, then a portion of our audience, not every single one of them will consider us high ni. And I think expanding that foothold is the way to navigate a business like that. You can see that with Qualtrics, you can see that with SurveyMonkey. Lots of companies are thinking about how to further unbundle that market for a very, very specific kind of customer. And that is what they're trying to do. They're trying to hit the high ni, even for that more generic workflow.
turns.zh: 例如，在Typeform公司，现在对我来说这已经是现实了。从技术层面讲，Typeform属于低频利基市场，或者说对所有人来说都是低频市场——这取决于它对客户的友好程度和易用性。作为产品策略的一部分，我正努力将其转变为高频利基市场，这才是最具生产力的位置。因此，对于营销人员和销售人员，我要确保他们首先想到我们。由于我们特别擅长面向客户的互动，如果他们认为我们是赢得新业务和赚钱的关键，那么我们的一部分受众（并非所有人）就会将我们视为高频利基市场。扩大这一市场份额正是经营此类业务的关键所在。你可以看到Qualtrics和SurveyMonkey的例子，许多公司都在思考如何为特定客户群体进一步拆分这个市场。这正是他们正努力做的。即便面对更通用的工作流程，他们也要瞄准高频利基市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. You also have this framework that I think you call the zone of benefit, which is around how much better does your solution have to be than the status quo? A lot of people are like, "Hey, look at this product, it's better than what you have now." And usually people are like, "Ah, whatever. It's good enough." And you've had some insights on just how much better it needs to be for people to care. Can you share that?
turns.zh: 这是一个绝佳的例子。你还有一个框架，我想你称之为"效益区"，即你的解决方案要比现状好多少倍？很多人会说，"嘿，看看这个产品，它比你现在用的要好"。但通常人们会说，"啊，随便啦，已经足够好了。" 你对让人们真正在意需要好到什么程度有深刻见解，能否分享一下？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Honestly, the reason I like being a product manager is on any given day, I'm drawing from anthropology, sociology, behavioral economics, leadership, communication skills. I'm trained, I have a master's in engineering, so I'm an engineer as well. I've done marketing and sales, so really pulling from so many things. And the reason I talk about the zone of benefit is ultimately what we're trying to do is impedance match technology to humans. That's it. If you really think about it, that's one essence of what we're trying to do. So the zone of benefit works as a framework because people will not pay for things that don't either really shrink the workflow that they're doing or doesn't give them superpower. So the same amount of time, but twice as much output. But the most important thing is that it has to be noticeable. (00:13:39): If you do something 20% better, often people just around you, just as a human, people don't notice. And so for a product to make a difference, it has to be at least two, three more X for people to say, "You know what? This is offering enough value for me to maybe make a switch in cost," and so on and so forth. And it really comes down to look, economic theory tells us that people work for leisure, they work enough to afford their leisure. It's sort of broad, and I know some people don't necessarily do that. Especially in the tech industry, people just love to work. But that is really it, when you think about eight billion people on the planet. And there's a lot of benefit really hones in on the fact that if you're going to help me work less, make about the same amount of money, then for me to notice you, you have to accelerate me by three times for me to care.
turns.zh: 说实话，我喜欢做产品经理的原因在于，每天我都在运用人类学、社会学、行为经济学、领导力和沟通技巧。我接受过工程学硕士训练，所以我也是工程师。我做过市场和销售工作，因此从多个领域汲取养分。谈到效益区，最终我们的目标是让技术与人类实现阻抗匹配。就是这样。如果你深入思考，这正是我们努力的核心所在。效益区作为一个框架之所以有效，是因为人们不会为那些既不能显著简化他们正在进行的工作流程，又不能赋予他们超能力的东西买单。同样的时间，但产出翻倍。但最重要的是，它必须引人注目。（00:13:39）：如果你把某件事做得好20%，通常身边的人——作为普通人——根本注意不到。为了让产品有所不同，它必须至少再提升两到三倍的效益，人们才会说：“你知道吗？这个为我提供了足够的价值，或许我可以换个更划算的选择。”等等。这归根结底是，经济理论告诉我们，人们工作是为了休闲，他们工作到足以负担得起休闲生活。这说法比较宽泛，我知道有些人不一定认同这一点。尤其是在科技行业，人们就是喜欢工作。但对于地球上80亿人来说，这才是关键所在。其中有很多益处都聚焦于这样一个事实：如果你能帮助我减少工作量，同时赚取差不多的钱，那么要让我注意到你，你就必须让我效率提升三倍，我才会感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. So three times. So the idea there is you should feel like this is three times more productive in the thing that I'm trying to do or saves me three times, I don't know, I do it three times faster.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。所以三次。关键是，你应该觉得这能让我的工作效率提高三倍，或者为我节省三倍的时间，我不知道，反正能让我做事快三倍。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, that's when people actually feel it and they feel it enough where they part with money.
turns.zh: 是啊，那时候人们真的能感受到这种效果，他们能感受到其中的价值，甚至愿意为此掏钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And I think what's cool about this is it helps you identify the ICP for your product if you're working a startup or even a new product within an existing product to figure out who exactly is going to most benefit from this. Is that part of this?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得这很酷的是，如果你是在创业公司工作，或者是在现有产品中开发新产品，它能帮助你确定产品的理想客户画像（ICP），找出谁最能从中受益。这是其中的一个关键点吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yes, yes. Your best customers aren't price sensitive for what you're shooting for because they get it. They fundamentally understand it. So yes, when you're shooting for ICPs, now every startup has marketing problems getting an audience problem. But once you start getting a decent audience, over 100 people or more, you should start to notice the people who are like, "You know what? This, I really care about this." And that starts to tell you a little bit about who's your target audience.
turns.zh: 对，对。对你所追求的客户来说，价格不是敏感点，因为他们能理解其中的价值。他们从根本上就懂。所以是的，当你致力于确定理想客户画像时，每个初创公司都会面临获取受众的营销难题。但一旦你成功吸引了一批体量较大的受众，比如超过100人或更多用户，你应该开始注意那些会说：“你知道吗？这个，我真的很在乎这个。” 这样的人会让你逐渐明白谁才是你的目标客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Would you be up for sharing the ICP of some of the companies you worked at? Just to give people a sense of what would be a good ICP.
turns.zh: 你能分享一下你曾工作过的公司的ICP吗？让大家对理想客户画像有个概念。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I think for Atlassian, it's really kind of obvious. It's developers mostly. But it's tech teams writ large because the fundamental of an R and D team is building stuff. And Jira helps the engineers who actually build stuff to track what they do and to give visibility to it so that they can be valuable to the organization. So that is incontroversial. So the ICP is really clear and have been clear for Atlassian for a very long time. Calendly is this weird company where people don't see all the value. People think it's just casual scheduling. But really the people who care about scheduling the most, and I don't mean calendaring. Calendaring is very different from scheduling. (00:16:25): The people who care about scheduling the most are salespeople because it's the lifeblood of them earning money and marketers, because it's the lifeblood of them maybe learning about their customer. Recruiters, because it's the lifeblood of them attracting and scheduling the people that they need to do their job. So Calendly's ICPs were people who were scheduling with people who were not in the organization for some business reason. Typeform is marketers mostly because Typeform exists to make the web talkative, to make it more human. And with Typeform, you can brand that conversation and actually make it conversational because one question at a time, the beautiful design. And so marketers feel like we help their websites talk to each other. Product people think we help their web apps talk to people they care about, UX people feel the same way. So those are some, I think the interesting thing is Twitter.
turns.zh: 我觉得Atlassian的ICP很明显，主要是开发者。但更广泛地说，是技术团队，因为研发团队的核心工作就是开发产品。Jira帮助实际开发产品的工程师追踪他们的工作进展，并提高工作可见度，这样他们才能为公司创造价值。这是毫无争议的。所以Atlassian的ICP一直很明确，而且很长一段时间以来都保持清晰。Calendly是个很奇特的公司，人们不理解它的全部价值。人们以为它只是随意安排日程的工具。但实际上，最在乎日程安排的人——我不是说日历管理，而是日程安排本身——是销售人员，因为这关乎他们赚钱的命脉；是市场人员，因为这关乎他们了解客户的命脉；是招聘人员，因为这关乎他们吸引和安排所需人才的命脉。所以Calendly的ICP是那些因业务需要与公司外部人员安排日程的人。而Typeform主要面向市场人员，因为Typeform的存在是为了让网络更具交互性，更人性化。通过Typeform，你可以给对话打上品牌标签，让对话真正具有互动性——一次一个问题，设计美观。所以市场人员觉得我们帮助他们的网站相互对话。产品经理认为我们帮助他们的应用与他们关心的用户对话。用户体验设计师也有同样的感受。所以这些都是有趣的例子，我觉得推特也是个很有意思的案例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to ask what the ICP for Twitter might be, still.
turns.zh: 我还想问一下，推特的ICP可能是什么。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: So Twitter is actually more fun in terms of ICP because first of all, I'll talk about the things that's not obvious about Twitter. 30% of Twitter's customer base were unseen, they were media organizations, people like the NFL, the NBA, HBO, who wanted their content to reach more people, to be in conversational spaces. And they were essentially business customers and not seen in the conversation pool, it's not obvious. But we interacted with them all the time and we rev shared ads for their videos, because we're making content all the time. And so Twitter was a way to extend the monetization of that content, that inventory that already had. But when you go to the consumer side of Twitter, who was the ICP? (00:18:25): Well, actually Twitter understood, and this is sort of reflected in what Elon Musk is doing these days, that he doesn't seem to understand. And if you ask anyone who was at Twitter, you'll see the understanding in their eyes and the fact that he doesn't understand, because Twitter's ICP is bifurcated. On one side, it is the most accomplished people in the world, the people who have something to say. This is why there's neuro Twitter, there's weather Twitter, there is cancer Twitter, and so on and so forth. In fact, if something breaks, some new innovation happens in the world, it probably breaks on Twitter before it breaks anywhere else, because these are people in informal communities following each other and sharing their results. (00:19:10): So basically there's this big circle of experts. We break down into celebrities, we break down into luminaries, leaders and so on and so forth. That's the ICP. Now how does Twitter work? These people attract the other 90% who listen to these people, but also they need to create their own informal communities around the things they're passionate about and have this mimetic relationship with the luminaries and the experts. And that is sort of the planet Twitter, experts on one side, humans who need to connect with the things they're passionate about, the people who are like them, that is the ICP of Twitter, the people who have something to say in those two categories.
turns.zh:
事实上，推特在ICP方面更有趣。首先，我要谈谈推特不为人熟知的方面。推特30%的客户群体是隐形的，他们是媒体机构，比如NFL、NBA、HBO等，这些机构希望自己的内容能被更多人看到，并参与到对话中。他们本质上是商业客户，但在对话池中并不显眼，这一点并不明显。不过我们一直与他们互动，为他们的视频分享广告，因为我们一直在创作内容。因此，推特是延长这些已有内容和库存的变现渠道。但当你转向推特的消费者端时，谁是ICP呢？（00:18:25）：其实推特明白这一点——这在埃隆·马斯克近期的行为中有所体现，他似乎并不理解这一点。如果你问任何曾在推特工作过的人，他们眼中会闪现出这种理解，而马斯克却不明白，因为推特的ICP是分裂的。一方面，这里聚集着世界上最有成就的人，他们有话要说。这就是为什么会有“神经推特”、“天气推特”、“癌症推特”等等。事实上，如果世界上有重大突破或创新，推特上很可能比其他任何地方更早出现相关讨论，因为这些人属于非正式社区，相互关注并分享成果。
（00:19:10）：所以基本上有一个庞大的专家圈子。我们可以将他们分为名人、杰出人物、领导者等。这些就是ICP。那么推特是如何运作的呢？这些人吸引了其他90%的人来聆听他们的声音，但他们也需要围绕自己热爱的事物创建自己的非正式社区，并与这些杰出人物和专家建立模仿关系。这就是推特的世界：一方面是专家，另一方面是需要与自己热爱的事物建立联系、寻找同类的人——这就是推特的ICP，属于这两类、有话要说的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you happy you're not working on Twitter anymore?
turns.zh: 你很高兴自己不再在推特工作了吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I am ecstatic, I'm ecstatic. It seems like such a shitshow, no shade on anything or anyone purposely. But look, what's happening is evident. So I don't think I have much to say about that.
turns.zh: 我太高兴了，太高兴了。看起来那简直就是一场闹剧，我没有恶意针对任何人或任何事。但看吧，现在发生的事情很明显。所以我觉得我对此没什么可说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, what a wild ride over there. Zooming out on the frameworks question, when I asked you ahead of our chat about what frameworks you love and anything you think would be interesting to share, you had a really interesting response and so I'd love for you to just share your perspective on frameworks broadly.
turns.zh: 是啊，那边真是疯狂了。退一步讲框架问题，我在我们的聊天前问你，你喜欢哪些框架，有没有什么你觉得分享起来会很有趣的，你的回答非常有趣，所以我希望你能广泛分享一下你对框架的看法。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah. Look, I'm two things simultaneously. One is actually, I like frameworks. The way that I try to express them is mental models because the essence of a framework and a mental model is that it is a shortcut. It packages some dense thinking into a way for you to approach a problem or to approach an opinion and so on and so forth. So I do collect them. But I think that what's important, I feel in product management, is to have the ability to understand the fundamentals or the empirical relationship that constructs a framework in the first place. In math, you would call it being able to derive the equation. And the reason that's important is because there's so much uncertainty in what we do. Product management isn't a science. In fact, programming isn't even a science really, because if it was, we'd treat it differently. So the art of building, say a software company that is profitable is not scientific. (00:21:36): There's a lot of uncertainty, a lot of unknowns, there's timing issues. So I guess while I love mental models, while I love frameworks, what I want people who listen to me and maybe listen to you to understand is you have to go deeper. Because as situations change, as an investor and advisor to startups, I advise differently if you are just starting, if you're in the middle, and if you're scaling. In the book that I'm writing on product, I actually make that distinction a lot in the book, which stage are you? Because then the thing that applies to you is different. If you understand the fundamentals, you'll be able to use frameworks in a much more productive way because you'll adapt it to your stage, you'll adapt it to the problem. And I think that's really important. I see lots of people using frameworks very blindly, and I think that's harmful to them and harmful to their businesses.
turns.zh: 是啊。你看，我同时有两个身份。首先，我确实喜欢框架。我试图用思维模型来表达它们，因为框架和思维模型的本质就是一种捷径。它将一些复杂的思考方式打包成一种方法，帮助你解决问题、理解观点等等。所以我确实会收集这些框架。但我认为，在产品管理中，更重要的是要具备理解构建框架的基本原理或经验关系的能力。在数学中，你会称之为能够推导出方程式。这一点之所以重要，是因为我们所做的事情存在太多不确定性。产品管理不是一门科学。事实上，编程甚至都算不上科学——如果编程是科学，我们对待它的方式就会截然不同。所以，建立一家盈利的软件公司的艺术，并非是科学。（00:21:36）：存在诸多不确定性，存在许多未知数，还有时机问题。所以我想，虽然我喜欢思维模型，喜欢框架，但我希望听我讲话的人——包括听你讲话的人——能明白一点：你必须深入思考。因为随着情况变化，作为初创公司的投资者和顾问，我会根据公司所处的不同阶段给出不同的建议——无论是刚起步、处于发展中期，还是在扩张阶段。在我正在写的产品管理书籍中，我在书中多次强调这个区别：你处于哪个阶段？因为适用于你的方法会有所不同。如果你理解了基本原理，你就能更有效地运用框架，因为你能将其适应自己的发展阶段，适应所面临的问题。我认为这点非常重要。我看到很多人盲目地使用框架，我认为这对他们和他们的业务都是有害的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a great segue to where I wanted to take us next, which is around the book that you're writing, which is my understanding is it's product management for product led growth. And I'm on your wait list to find out when it's out, and I saw that the other day you asked people for their advice on what to call the book. Do you have any favorites at this point of what you might title it?
turns.zh: 接下来我要引出我想探讨的下一个话题，那就是你正在写的那本书。据我了解，书的主题是产品管理与产品驱动型增长。我在你的邮件列表上，等着书出版的消息。前几天我看到你征求读者对书名建议的推文。目前你有没有特别喜欢的书名？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Well first of all, there are two things happening with the book. One is I believe PLG is, I have maybe a different definition of PLG, but I think the way that we are basically adapting products to the consumer or to the business professional and using the product itself to sell the value proposition is really key to transitioning from what we used to do 20 years ago to today. Basically, I think even enterprise companies will tend towards a consumer type product management over the next decade than the other way around, that's my bet. And so let's call that PLG, just writ large. And also I think product management is set for growth. So obviously that's good for you, Lenny, because everyone needs to know how to do this. (00:23:39): It's an integrative art within building software and software is seeding the world, the book, I want to get very practical. What matters about doing those two things well, and the best titles coming up are, my original title was Building Rocket Ships. So it's like how do you think through all the different things you need to build a really successful software company? Think about the practice, think about the business, meld those two things together. So a lot of people love that title. Well, there's a huge variation in submissions. So I think we're going to do that one more time and offer more options before we nail down the title of the book, so still TBD.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，关于这本书，有两件事值得探讨。第一点是，我认为PLG（产品生命周期管理）很重要。我可能对PLG有不同的定义，但我认为我们将产品适应消费者或商业用户，并利用产品本身来传递价值主张的方式，确实是从20年前到今天转型关键的要素。基本来说，我认为未来十年，即使是企业公司也会倾向于采用消费者类型的产品管理模式，而不是反过来——这就是我的预测。所以让我们把这部分称为PLG的大写版本。另外，我认为产品管理领域将迎来快速发展。这对莱尼来说显然是个好消息，因为每个人都需要掌握这方面的技能。（00:23:39）在软件开发领域，产品管理是一门综合性艺术，而软件正在改变世界。这本书，我想写得非常实用。在这两件事上做得好至关重要，目前最受欢迎的书名是《打造火箭飞船》。所以这本书的核心在于，如何统筹考虑打造一家成功软件公司所需的各种要素？既要考虑实践，又要兼顾商业逻辑，将两者完美融合。很多人都喜欢这个书名。不过投稿内容差异巨大。所以我们打算再征集一轮意见，然后再确定书名，所以目前还没最终定下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool, all right. I'm excited to see where you land. So let's just spend some time on PLG. I feel like this is your bread and butter as a product leader. You've worked at some of the most successful PLG companies and I think you have some of the most unique perspectives on what works and doesn't work. And I saw you shared a preview of what you're going to be sharing the book, and so there's a few things there that I thought were really interesting that I haven't seen other places when it comes to PLG. So I was just going to dig into it-
turns.zh: 太棒了，好吧。我很期待看到你的成果。接下来我们就专注PLG吧。我觉得这对你来说是强项，毕竟你曾在PLG领域最成功的公司工作过，对其中的成败秘诀有着独特见解。我看到你分享了新书的预览，其中有几点观点在PLG领域很新颖，别处难得一见。所以我特别想深入探讨一下——

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yay.
turns.zh: 太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. The first is this framing that you had for where to start and how to focus with your PLG problem. And you described it as starting with a sharp problem. Can you talk about what that means?
turns.zh: 当然。首先，你提到的如何从PLG问题入手并聚焦核心的框架。你说要从一个尖锐的问题入手，能具体解释一下吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, so I'm trying to connect dots. The sharp problem is a little bit of that whole quadrant framework, which is what problem are you going to work on? I think that problems have predictive power of success if you actually solve the problem. And this is different from, I have an idea, yeah. I think that a lot of innovation can come from inspiration, but the best inspiration comes from understanding customers and their problems. So my advice to founders is pick a problem that is materially felt by your customers, pain points that steal their time, their energy, their money, their focus, the inability to afford their leisure. If you can solve those kinds of problems, and look, I know that it's broad, because it requires insight. The best founders often are people who felt a problem, understand it, understand that it's really difficult, and understand that there may be like five, 10, 20 billion people who feel it and they don't want to solve that problem versus I feel a problem, but only 100,000 people care. In which case, maybe it's not that intense anyway, unless you can charge them thousands and thousands of dollars. (00:26:22): So pick those kinds of problems. If you have the narrative in your head that if you really solve this, people will pony up. That's what I ask people to find. Too many of us just have a sharp idea. Look, I've built a startup on a non-sharp problem, and I knew how it felt. Well, I also know working in companies that are solving sharp problems how it feels, it's a huge tailwind to do that. In fact, when you work on sharp problems, it's hard to fail because you can make mistakes and the customer's obsession will carry you, but if you work on something that doesn't have a sharp problem, mistakes can kill you because essentially you're having to pay a lot for marketing, you're having to pay a lot for word of mouth. People, when they get poor, they don't care about it, like recessions.
turns.zh:
是的，我正在努力理清思路。关键问题在于整个象限框架——你要解决什么样的问题？我认为，如果你能真正解决问题，就能预见成功的可能性。这和"我有个想法"不同。很多创新源自灵感，但最棒的灵感往往来自对客户及其问题的深刻理解。因此，我给创业者的建议是：选择一个客户切实感受到的痛点——那些耗费他们时间、精力、金钱、注意力，甚至让他们无力享受休闲时光的问题。若能解决这类问题（我知道这听起来很宏大，因为它需要洞察力），往往能收获最佳创意。最优秀的创业者往往亲身感受到问题所在，理解其复杂性，意识到可能有50亿、100亿人面临同样的痛点，而非只有10万人感兴趣。除非你能向他们收取高额费用，否则这种痛点可能并不足够强烈。

（00:26:22）所以要选择这类问题。当你脑海中浮现"如果能真正解决这个问题，人们就会买单"的场景时，那才是我希望人们去寻找的。太多人只是一时灵光一闪。看，我曾基于一个不算尖锐的问题创办过一家初创公司，当时我深有体会。但在解决尖锐问题的公司工作时，你能感受到巨大的助力——即使犯错，客户的执着也会支撑你前进。而面对不尖锐的问题，错误却可能致命，因为你不得不投入大量营销成本，靠口碑传播。人们在经济低迷时往往漠不关心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to something you mentioned earlier about just how much pain it needs to be for people to care or how much pain it needs to solve versus the status quo, I think is a really important element of this. I think most founders like, no, I need to solve a problem. But usually it's not painful enough or it's not solving it enough, given either an example of something that you've tried or you've seen of just like that was a sharpish problem but not sharp enough and people didn't care, either a company worked or a startup you advised of just like, okay, it wasn't sharp enough.
turns.zh: 回到你之前提到的——问题必须足够令人痛苦，人们才会关注，或者与现状相比有多大改进——我认为这是一个关键要素。多数创业者都想"不，我要解决问题"。但通常问题不够痛切，或者解决力度不够。无论是基于你尝试过的例子，还是见过的其他案例——比如某个创业公司试图解决尖锐问题却失败，或者你指导的初创公司因不够尖锐而失败。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I don't want to create enemies because I know a lot of founders. But here's one, here's one. I don't know if you remember during the pandemic, this venture studio by I think one of the ex founders of Evernote created mmhmm camera, remember that?
turns.zh: 我不想树敌，因为我认识很多创业者。但这里有个例子，不知道你是否还记得疫情期间，由Evernote前创始人之一创立的风险投资工作室开发的mmhmm相机，还记得吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah, absolutely. Yeah, great video.
turns.zh: 哦，对，绝对是。是的，视频很棒。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: It was fun, but I don't think it was a sharp problem. It was fun, but yeah, it didn't change the world of your Zoom camera. It didn't change the world of your collaboration. And so I think that's one example of a non-sharp problem, for example, for most people.
turns.zh: 很有趣，但我不认为这是尖锐问题。很有趣，但没能改变你Zoom相机的世界，也没改变你的协作方式。所以我认为这就是一个非尖锐问题的例子，至少对大多数人来说是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are signs that it's sharp enough, just like in your experience? I know you talked about it steals your time, energy, money focused. What are flags that this is sharp enough in your experience?
turns.zh: 根据你的经验，怎样判断问题足够尖锐？我知道你提到过它耗费时间、精力、金钱、注意力。在你看来，哪些迹象表明问题足够尖锐？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I think there are two ways to think about it. If you are in the trenches as a founder, the easiest way to map out a sharp problem is draw the current approximate average workflow for your target customer, at least what you think is a target, and then draw the workflow after they've used your software and see how much shorter it is, yes or no. And then try to measure those lines. If you draw them as horizontal lines, try to measure those lines and see if it's much shorter. If it's 2X shorter, 3X shorter, so let's say pre-customer, that is the best way to hone in on it. Post customer, you should talk to the people who are most enthusiastic and derive their workflow and their workflow change and try to measure that. I think that's how you figure out if it's a sharp problem or not. (00:29:37): The other thing that we talk about in startup super early stage world is, I call it the whites of their eyes. When you take a problem and you share it with someone who it's going to affect their workflow, and I use the word workflow a ton because I don't use specs anymore or use cases, I think workflows are the unit of productivity. When you see people's eyes get big and they expose more whites to you, you're probably onto something. It's not enough, that's not a workflow thing, that's an excitement thing. But people often react that way when you're solving a really sharp problem for them. And then people spontaneously bring up money, it's like when can I pay? When can I... Those kinds of things give you an indication.
turns.zh:
我认为有两种思考方式。如果你作为创始人亲身经历创业过程，最简单的方法就是描绘出目标客户当前大致的工作流程——至少是你所设想的目标客户的工作流程——然后再描绘出他们使用你的软件后的工作流程，看看是否缩短了很多。接着尝试测量这些线段。如果你把它们画成水平线，再去测量，发现确实缩短了很多。比如说，如果缩短了两倍、三倍，那么在产品尚未面向客户之前，这就是锁定核心问题的绝佳方法。面向客户后，你应该与最热情的用户交流，了解他们的工作流程变化并进行测量。我认为这就是判断问题是否尖锐的关键。

（00:29:37）：在创业初期阶段，我们常讨论的一个现象，我称之为“眼白部分”。当你向将受你的产品影响的人提出一个问题时，如果你看到他们的眼睛突然放大，眼白部分暴露得更多，这通常意味着你找到了关键点。光是这样还不够，这不是关于工作流程的问题，而是他们对解决方案的兴奋反应。当你为他们解决一个真正尖锐的问题时，人们往往会自发地提起资金问题，比如“我什么时候能付款？”“什么时候能用上？”这些反应能给你提供重要线索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two other versions of the showing more whites of your eyes, which I love. Two other versions of that I've heard is one is you see their pupils dilate and they're just like, "Whoa, I need this now." And then the other is someone described it as, you see this nod of as you're talking, they're just like, "Oh, I get it. I get this." And then they're like, "Okay, we need this in our company."
turns.zh: 关于“眼白部分”的另外两个版本，我也很喜欢。其中一个版本是看到对方瞳孔放大，他们会感叹：“哇，我现在就需要这个！”另一个版本是有人描述说：当你说话时，他们会频频点头：“哦，我懂了。我明白了。然后他们会说：“好，我们公司也需要这个。”

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I'm a little over those ones because sometimes it's just excitement and just noise. And so the things I said previously about workflow compression or capability inflation, I think those are more reliable, which is all about customer research and customer conversations. That's what I would focus on. Yeah, I'm saying all this from mistakes I've made, basically. So I feel like this is scar tissue, which is what I'm trying to pour into the book.
turns.zh: 我对这些反应有点审慎，因为有时这只是兴奋带来的噪音。所以我之前提到的那些方法，比如工作流程压缩或能力提升，我认为这些更可靠。这都与客户研究和客户对话有关。这才是我真正关注的重点。是的，我说这些都是从我自己犯过的错误中总结出来的。所以我觉得这些都是宝贵的经验，我正把它们写进书里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of talking to customers, another one of your big bullet points in the book is around continuous customer discovery, and I'm curious what you found to be successful in actually doing that. A lot of people talk about it when you keep talking to customers, get feedback constantly. What actually works in your experience?
turns.zh: 说到与客户沟通，书中另一个重要的要点是持续的客户发现。我很好奇，在实际操作中，你发现哪些方法是有效的。很多人谈到要不断与客户沟通，持续获取反馈。根据你的经验，哪些方法确实有效？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, I feel like all of park management is about discovery these days. Everyone talks about it, and I want to make a distinction. I think discovery is when you use customer conversations to understand a very specific thing that you want to optimize further workflow that you want to optimize further. And then you call the people who are most likely to be affected and you do use various research strategies to talk to them. There's a version of that also that is what I call continuous conversations, which is a Calendly and a Typeform, which we'll do more and more of. You should organize it so that your PMs, your designers, your engineering managers and your PMMs are constantly talking to customers by default. Meaning that customer conversations show up on their calendar every week automagically, without them getting involved. And then they're trained on how to have the conversation, because the death of customer discovery is friction. If you ask individuals to do customer discovery, they will not do customer discovery. (00:32:49): This is the thing that dies in an innovative company because it's very difficult to actually talk to the right customer, not talk to any customer, talk list of the right customer continuously. But there's a third thing that I like to talk about, which is customer listening. In fact, I'm going to talk about this at industry in October, the PM Conference. Customer listening is different. It's not really discovery. It is the scarfing up of customer signals that are happening constantly anyway. So people are talking on social, people are talking on app stores and G2 crowd. If you have a instrumented churn survey, people are talking. If you have NPS, people are not only giving you the scores where they're putting in the verbatims. If you have a bug report, which we had at Atlassian, people are filing bugs, developers love to file bugs, so of course we have that for that audience. And then if you go to Zendesk and customer support, people are either talking about one thing all the time or a range of things, and you can see the frequency distribution. (00:34:01): And of course in Salesforce, you have closed one. These are all things happening no matter what you do. Whether you're listening or not, you're getting these signals. One of the big, hairy, audacious goals of product management is being able to process these signals efficiently. We did it in a certain way at Calendly, which I drew a rig together through workflows and Slack, and then having individuals triage those things. And if you can do that hard and at industry, I'll talk a little bit about how to do it. It's not exactly discovery. It is what matters. Our job is to meld customer delight with business ambition. And it feels essential beyond discovery that you are listening and you're understanding what matters from a customer delight perspective. And I don't think many of us do this really well. I've tried to do it everywhere I've gone, Twitter, Atlassian, Calendly, now at Typeform. But it still feels like something that the industry can get better at.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得如今整个产品管理领域都热衷于“客户洞察”这个概念。每个人都在谈论它，但我想对此做个区分。在我看来，真正的客户洞察是指通过与客户的对话来理解某个具体问题，进而优化工作流程。然后，你会联系最可能受影响的人群，并运用各种研究策略与他们展开交流。还有一种类似的做法，我称之为“持续对话”，比如使用Calendly和Typeform工具——我们会越来越多地应用这些工具。理想情况下，产品经理、设计师、工程经理和项目管理经理应当默认就与客户保持沟通。也就是说，每周自动在他们的日历中安排客户对话，无需他们主动参与。同时，他们需要接受如何有效沟通的培训，因为客户洞察的核心在于消除阻碍。如果让个人去主动开展客户洞察，他们往往会敷衍了事。

（00:32:49）这正是创新型公司容易失败的关键点——真正与合适的客户对话、持续获取客户反馈并非易事。还有第三个概念——客户倾听。事实上，我将在10月的PM大会上重点探讨这个话题。客户倾听与传统的客户洞察不同，它不是主动探索，而是持续收集本就存在的客户信号。例如，用户在社交媒体、应用商店和G2 Crowd平台上的讨论；仪表化的流失率调查；NPS评分背后的真实反馈；Atlassian内部的bug报告系统（开发者热衷于提交bug报告）；Zendesk客户支持数据中的频繁反馈模式；Salesforce中的客户成交数据……无论你是否主动倾听，这些信号都会源源不断地传来。

（00:34:01）产品管理的核心挑战在于高效处理这些信号。我们在Calendly通过工作流和Slack搭建了处理机制，并安排专人进行分类处理。在Industry大会上，我将详细分享相关实践。这并非传统意义上的客户洞察，而是至关重要的客户倾听。我们的职责是将客户满意度与商业目标相结合。除了洞察能力，更重要的是持续倾听客户声音，从客户满意度的角度理解关键需求。我认为多数从业者在这方面做得不够。我曾在Twitter、Atlassian、Calendly等平台反复实践，如今在Typeform也持续探索，但整个行业仍有提升空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on advice that Teresa Torres teaches around continuous customer discovery. And she actually had a really good tactic, that I'll share here that stuck with me, about how to actually do this. So the way she recommends companies do this is have a little popup on your site asking visitors like we'd love to talk to you and get your feedback on our product. And it just links them to a Calendly to book a meeting, and that's how it shows up on the calendar.
turns.zh: 这涉及到特蕾莎·托雷斯（Teresa Torres）关于持续客户探索的建议。她确实有一个非常好的策略，我在这里分享一下，让我印象深刻，关于如何具体做到这一点。因此，她建议公司在网站上设置一个弹窗，询问访客：“我们很乐意与您交流，并获取您对我们产品的反馈。” 然后将他们引导至Calendly平台预约会议，这就是它在日历上显示的方式。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, that's what we did at Calendly. But I will say, so a couple of caveats, we did that in the community. We had community at calendly.com and we understood that that was a self-selected group. But it was still important to talk to them because they were still representative. And of course you should do it in a product. The challenge of that approach is always is it the right customer? And the pro/con of that is talking to one customer is useless, talking to 100 is super useful. And so the challenge is are you targeting the right person? (00:36:09): So some intelligence upfront and who to show it to and why you're showing it to them, so that they can come is interesting. Very particularly effective by the way for growth, because if people don't activate or churn, they don't want to talk to you. But if you can present that thing in their activation or conversion journey, they might actually talk to you. And so that's really key. So I 100% agree with Teresa, that's exactly what you should do for not even, I wouldn't even call it discoveries for listening, and some of it can be discovery. Yeah, I think that's exactly what you should do.
turns.zh: 是的，这正是我们在Calendly所做的。但我要说明几个注意事项：我们是在社区中这样做的。我们在calendly.com上建立了社区，我们知道这是一个自愿加入的群体。但与他们交流仍然很重要，因为他们仍然具有代表性。当然，你也应该在产品中这样做。这种方法的挑战始终在于：客户是否合适？其利弊在于，与一个客户交流毫无意义，与100个客户交流则非常有用。因此，关键在于你是否针对了正确的人？（00:36:09）：所以事先要进行一些分析，确定向谁展示，以及为什么要向他们展示，这样他们才会前来，这很有趣。顺便说一句，这对增长特别有效，因为如果人们不激活或流失，他们就不想与你交流。但如果你能在他们的激活或转化过程中呈现这些内容，他们可能会真正与你交流。因此，这真的很关键。所以我完全同意特蕾莎的观点，这正是你应该做的，甚至我不会称之为探索，而是倾听，而其中一些也可以被视为探索。是的，我认为这正是你应该做的。

turns.en: As you're talking I'm realizing I'm using most of the products you help build. I'm on Twitter a lot. I use Calendly a lot. I use Typeform as my default survey tool.

turns.en: I saw that, my team is really excited that you're using Typeform.
