turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Let me talk about a few fundamentals. Onboarding is a substitute for sales and all these account management teams for millions of customers. The task is how do you make it approximate a human and how friendly a human is and how approachable a human is? Because if you can do that, then you can process thousands and thousands of customers very quickly. Onboarding is an exercise in understanding the mindset of a buyer, of an evaluator. It's nothing more than that. Meaning that the province of understanding is social psychology, it's not really product, it's biopsychology. And guess who knows a lot about this stuff, it's people in the offline industry. The people who stock shelves, the people who provide inventory online and so on and so forth. They are extraordinarily good at this. So the reason I say this is to divert people who are [inaudible 00:40:00] to really find where to source their inspiration from for onboarding, first of all. (00:40:06): If you think about this as intentful in that way, which is people come not knowing anything about you and in a progressively developed confidence that you are the tool of choice, you then have to break it down into how does that journey go through a mind, the average mind anyway, and how do you assist each part? One is value proposition, understanding, one is trying to see if it's simple enough and provides enough value. One is kicking tires and one is making the choice that this is something I'm going to go forward with. How does your onboarding support hit all of these things? Now I think there are two parts of onboarding. One is mandatory, the setup, it has to be spare. I try not to make it more than three screens, but it's about how do you say what this does and provide the essential setup that your customer needs to be successful? (00:41:05): At Calendly, for example, we asked them about connecting their calendar and setting some defaults. Is it 9:00 to 5:00 or whatever that is? Those two things set up all the future success. And if we made it optional, more people would fail. So it's information and the essential setup, and it should be as short as possible. Then there's a whole other set of things that should be optional because they're not necessary for everyone to be successful, but they're beneficial if people are curious. And also, it can be what we call a random access, so people can get back to it any time they want, if they're feeling help. And so if you divide onboarding into those two things and then figure out what to put in one and what to put in the other, I think you can be quite successful. And this is just the tip of the iceberg that I get into in the book.
turns.zh:
让我来谈谈几个基础问题。入职流程是销售的替代品，也是数百万客户的账户管理团队所承担的任务。关键在于如何让它尽可能贴近人性化，让用户感觉友好且易于接近？因为如果能做到这一点，就能快速处理数千名客户的需求。入职流程实质上是理解买家和评估者的思维模式。这就是全部要点所在。理解的范畴属于社会心理学，而非产品设计或生物心理学。猜猜谁在这方面深有研究？就是线下行业的人——货架陈列员、线上库存管理员等等。他们在这方面堪称行家。说这些是想提醒那些（00:40:00）过度纠结于技术细节的人，要先找准入职流程的灵感源泉。

（00:40:06）：若从用户意图角度思考，用户对你的产品一无所知，但逐渐建立信任并选择你作为首选工具。那么关键在于如何让用户在大脑中完成这个认知过程，特别是普通用户的心理路径。首先要理解价值主张，评估是否足够简洁且价值显著。接着是试用阶段，最后是做出决策。你的入职流程如何全方位支持这些阶段？

入职流程可分为两部分：一是必须完成的核心设置，需保持简洁。我尽量控制在三个页面以内。二是可选内容，满足用户个性化需求。例如，Calendly会引导用户关联日历并设置默认设置，如工作时间9点至5点等。这些基础设置对用户成功至关重要，若设为可选，成功率会大打折扣。因此，核心信息和必要设置要简洁明了，并尽可能缩短流程。可选内容可供用户根据需求自由选择，支持随机访问功能，让用户随时获取帮助。将入职流程分为两部分，再合理分配内容，成功几率会大大提升。这只是我书中探讨的冰山一角。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any examples of really big onboarding wins, things that really helped with conversion or activation that come to mind?
turns.zh: 有没有特别成功的入职流程案例，能有效提升转化率或激活率？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Well, I think keep it short is one big win. The fewer things, the better, that are essential, that everyone has to go through. It's unclear if all those clickthroughs go here, go here, and all those things work-
turns.zh: 简洁高效就是一大成功之道。核心流程要简明易懂，人人必经。用户是否会逐项点击指引？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The wizards, yeah.
turns.zh: 比如引导式向导。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah. The wizards have had, in my experience, limited benefit. So much as just directing people to the one thing that they need to do post mandatory onboarding. Having examples, not 10, one or two of what good looks like is particularly powerful because it's mimetic. People see, oh, okay, this is exactly what I'm shooting for, is very powerful. In terms of trial and conversion, letting people understand and being very clear about where they are in the trial cycle, whether you want them to pay for it now or they need to pay for it later, after seven days. Having them understand that really clearly so they know where they are versus they feel like they're completely at sea, I think is very important for conversion. (00:43:07): I think there are a few things like that, but I also want to mention that it's different for every product. Depending on where you are in the quadrant and the amount of augmentation and problem solving and how sharp the problem is, you might want to adjust your approach. And this is the kind of thing that there's some fundamentals, but it's not necessarily this one size fits all. In fact, at Typeform, we're trying to maybe invent a new twist on freemium just because of some of the things we're seeing for our particular customers. And so yeah, these are for me, some new learning as well as I go through each different product.
turns.zh:
是的。以我的经验来看，向导功能的益处有限。它们主要就是把人们引导到强制入职后需要做的一件事上。提供示例——不是10个，而是1-2个优秀案例——尤其有效，因为这种示范效应很强。人们看到后，会觉得，哦，原来这就是我要努力达成的目标，这效果很棒。在试用和转化方面，确保用户理解并清楚自己在试用周期中的位置——无论是现在付费，还是七天后再付费——让他们清楚自己的处境，而不是感到迷茫，这对转化至关重要。  
（00:43:07）：我认为还有一些类似的做法，但每个产品都不同。取决于你所处的象限、产品对用户问题的解决程度以及问题的紧迫性，你可能需要调整方法。这类问题有一些基本原则，但并非放之四海而皆准。事实上，我们在Typeform正试图为免费增值模式开创新思路，因为我们为特定客户观察到了一些问题。因此，对我来说，每个不同产品都是新的学习机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines of onboarding activation and getting a user activated is really important. And I'm curious, do you have an example of what an activation milestone was at Calendly or Twitter or a Typeform? Just to give people a sense of like here's a good example of an activated user milestone.
turns.zh: 围绕激活用户这一点，入职激活和用户激活非常重要。我很好奇，你们在Calendly、Twitter或Typeform有没有激活里程碑的例子？让人们了解一个激活用户的优秀范例。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I think this goes back to people, the Pendos and the Amplitudes of this world. You have to think through your aha journey. Like at Calendly and also at Typeform we have three thresholds of increasing activation. And we just try to make sure that people go through each one as many people as possible. And frankly, we try to figure the drop-off between the increasing definitions of activation. So at Calendly we want to make sure you've created your first meeting. But then if you've created five within a week, that's really much more powerful. At Typeform, it's really about have you published the form and have you gotten responses? And have you gone to look at what the responses mean in the insights page, for example. (00:44:52): At Twitter it is are you following anyone or are you being followed? Because that verb, follow, is the way you start to construct your informal community. Remember what I said is Twitter is for people who want informal community around a topic that is not... Facebook is about who do you know, Twitter is about who do you want to know? Who's passionate about what you're passionate about? And so if you haven't set up your follow graph at all, you're not going to really activate. It's not going to be compelling for you.
turns.zh:
我认为这要回归到Pendo和Amplitude这样的公司。你们必须仔细规划用户的aha时刻。比如在Calendly和Typeform，我们设定了三个递增的激活门槛，并努力让尽可能多的用户通过每个门槛。坦白说，我们还试图了解每个激活定义之间的转化率差异。在Calendly，我们希望确保用户创建了第一个会议。但如果用户一周内创建了五个会议，效果会更显著。在Typeform，关键在于用户是否发布了表单并获得了反馈，以及是否在洞察页面查看了反馈数据。  
（00:44:52）：在Twitter上，关键在于用户是否关注了别人或者被别人关注。因为“关注”这个动作是构建非正式社区的起点。记住我之前说过的，Twitter是为那些希望围绕某个非正式话题建立社区的人而设计的，而Facebook则侧重于社交关系。Twitter的核心是让人们围绕感兴趣的话题找到志同道合的人。所以如果用户根本没有建立关注图，他们就很难真正激活起来。这对他们来说毫无吸引力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, those are great examples. It's funny hearing that Twitter activation milestone out of context sounds, so creepy. Have you followed anyone or is anyone following you?
turns.zh: 太棒了，这些例子都很棒。脱离上下文听Twitter的激活里程碑，听起来有点吓人。你有没有关注过别人或者被别人关注过？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, because a lot of people go in and then they tweet into the void or they don't feel like they have a voice. But that's not the most important thing. Most important thing is are you getting content that you are interested in that makes you want to come back and see more of it and follow is a huge part of doing that.
turns.zh: 是啊，因为很多人加入后要么在社交媒体上发些没人回应的内容，要么觉得自己没有发声的机会。但这都不是最重要的。最重要的是，你能否获得感兴趣的内容，让用户愿意回来看更多内容并关注，这才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Just on the point of Twitter, I don't know if this goes anywhere, but it's crazy how it keeps going no matter how much destruction is happening all around, employees-
turns.zh: 是啊，说到推特，我不知道它能走多远，但令人惊讶的是，无论周围有多大的动荡，它依然能继续运转，员工们——

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Oh, you want me to talk about that? Because I want to talk about this.
turns.zh: 哦，你想让我谈这个？因为我想谈谈这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please, let's do it.
turns.zh: 拜托，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: So one of the things they, I don't want to say they, one of the things I learned early on is network effects.
turns.zh: 所以他们（我不想说是“他们”），我早期学到的一件事就是网络效应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Network effects, let me define it. Network effects is when you create value for passive members by other people joining the network. So I am by myself, I have done nothing. I'm at home, chilling, but one person joins the network and immediately I gain benefit, okay. So think about Facebook. If there are eight billion people on Facebook, it means that all of a sudden I can reach everyone on the planet. And so the more people on Facebook, the more it's valuable to me regardless of my effort. That's network effect. If I'm into Word, word processor, Microsoft Word, and the more people who use that file format, it means that the more Word documents I can read. (00:47:05): And so I did nothing, so by increasing the people adoption of Word, I gain benefit. Network effect, that's what it is. So Twitter and then this is the mental model of critical mass, network effect is about critical mass. You hit a critical mass and sometimes that's not mathematically defined, and then you've hit network effect because people want to come because people are already there. So Twitter has hit critical mass and lots of your favorite social networks. Network effects is a feature by itself, and it's the most powerful feature. A good way to illustrate the power of network effects is Twitter did not die because Threads came about, that's the power of network effect. In fact, the last telegram was sent in 2016, over 100 years after it was invented because of network effects. It had to be manually closed down. (00:48:03): I believe Friendster is still alive, so we have to be really clear that it's really hard to kill a network effects business. Now how do you actually accomplish it if you were to accomplish it? Well, the revenue side of any social network is vulnerable to attack. So for example, if advertisers stop being on Twitter, for example, they're not gone because again, network effects affects them. They want to go where the eyeballs are. But if for some reason they disappeared, while the people will continue to come, the ability to have money to improve the network will disappear. And that is a negative spiral. What is very, very hard to kill business, it's hard to kill software that's reached network effect, although you can kill businesses that have reached network effect.
turns.zh: 网络效应，让我来定义一下。网络效应是指，当其他人加入网络时，你为被动成员创造价值。所以我独自一人，在家放松，但一个人加入网络，我立即就能获益。那么想想Facebook。如果Facebook有80亿用户，那意味着我突然就能联系到全球所有人。所以Facebook的用户越多，对我来说就越有价值，无论我自己如何努力。这就是网络效应。如果我用微软Word处理文档，使用该文件格式的人越多，我就越能读取更多Word文档。（00:47:05）：所以我什么都没做，但随着更多人采用Word，我就能获益。这就是网络效应。Twitter和这种临界质量的心理模型，网络效应就是关于临界质量的。当你达到临界质量时（有时这不是数学定义的），你就触发了网络效应，因为人们想加入，因为其他人已经在那里。所以Twitter已经达到了临界质量，许多你喜欢的社交网络也是如此。网络效应本身就是一项功能，而且是最强大的功能。说明网络效应威力的一个好例子是，Threads的出现并没有让Twitter消亡，这就是网络效应的力量。事实上，电报最后一次发送是在2016年，距离它发明已经超过100年了，因为网络效应。它不得不被手动关闭。（00:48:03）：我相信Friendster仍然存在，所以我们必须清楚，杀死一个网络效应业务非常困难。现在如果你要做到这一点，你该怎么做呢？嗯，任何社交网络的收入端都容易受到攻击。例如，如果广告商停止在Twitter上投放广告，他们不会消失，因为网络效应仍然影响着他们。他们想去有眼球的地方。但如果他们因为某种原因消失了，虽然用户会继续来，但用于改进网络的资金就会消失。这就是一个负向螺旋。真正难以杀死的业务，是达到网络效应的软件，尽管你可以杀死已经达到网络效应的业务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really important and interesting insight. I think what's even especially interesting about Twitter is Elon and the team have removed every other benefit of Twitter, like the brand, gone, employees, 80% gone. Every part of it is being cut off, except for the network effects, and so it's a really cool case study. Dan Hockenmaier tweeted this, was a previous guest, of just like it's a good case study of what is just the power of just network effects.
turns.zh: 这真是一个非常重要且有趣的见解。我认为Twitter特别有趣的地方在于，埃隆和他的团队剥离了Twitter的其他优势——品牌消失、员工离职，80%的员工被裁掉。除了网络效应外，其他一切都在被切断，因此这是一个非常棒的案例研究。丹·霍肯迈尔（Dan Hockenmaier）曾在推特上发文，他曾是嘉宾，称这是一个关于网络效应力量的绝佳案例研究。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: That's right. I did a really interesting course at Berkeley Business School, asked about technology companies and so on, and this is a perfect case study on network effect. The best I've ever seen. It is incredible.
turns.zh: 没错。我在伯克利商学院上过一门非常有趣的课程，研究科技公司等领域，而Twitter的案例研究堪称关于网络效应的完美范例。这是我见过最出色的案例之一，真是令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's wild Threads isn't able to get there quickly, unlike what it felt like initially.
turns.zh: 是啊，让人惊讶的是Threads没能迅速取得成功，不像最初预期的那样。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Threads will prosper, I believe. And again, it'll just be another click for advertisers who understand the Facebook marketplace versus Twitter ad marketplace is much harder to access. And so I think the way Threads wins is the revenue spiral versus the pure activity spiral.
turns.zh: 我相信Threads会发展得很好。我再说一次，广告商会发现，与Facebook市场相比，Twitter广告市场更难触达。这意味着Threads的成功之路将是收入螺旋式上升，而非单纯的活跃用户数量攀升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Where essentially they find ways to, even with lower base, generate revenue, which drives advertisers, drives more investment.
turns.zh: 有意思。基本上他们能找到办法，即便在用户基础较低的情况下也能创造收入，从而吸引广告商和更多投资。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Correct, correct, correct.
turns.zh: 没错，没错，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. All right. That'll be fun story to watch. Kind of along those same lines, I want to chat about virality a little bit. You worked on some of those viral products out there in B2C, I guess Twitter is an example, but also in B2B, which is really rare and interesting. And I know there's no silver bullet for increasing virality, but everyone's always wondering, how do I increase the virality of my product? So I'm curious, anything you could share, any tactics that you've seen work to increase the virality, especially of a B2B product?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好吧。这会是个很有趣的发展故事。顺便说一下，我想聊聊病毒式传播。您曾参与过一些B2C领域的病毒式产品，比如Twitter，但B2B领域的病毒式传播案例更是罕见且有趣。我知道增加病毒式传播没有万能法宝，但大家总想知道如何提升产品病毒性。所以我很好奇，您能否分享一些成功的策略，特别是针对B2B产品？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Well, as is my style, I want people to understand what virality is in the first place because I think people have misconceptions about it. People think virality is some Hotmails tag at the bottom that says, we'll get a free account. Virality is really when the word of mouth of a product is high quality. That's really the essence of it. Let me rephrase that. It's when customers market your product. And that is incredibly powerful, but also that's incredibly actionable, if that makes sense. There are products who try to be viral just for what I call synthetic virality that fail. Because in the end, if you're synthetically viral and people get to the product and it sucks, that's it. That's the end. Even Hotmail, for example, people talk about the viral tag. I don't know, you know what I'm talking about? Because I-
turns.zh: 嗯，按照我的风格，我首先想让大家理解病毒式传播到底是什么，因为我觉得人们对它存在误解。人们以为病毒式传播就是Hotmail底部有个标签写着“免费账户”之类的。但病毒式传播的本质是产品口碑的高质量。这才是关键所在。让我换个说法。就是让客户主动推广你的产品。这非常强大，也非常可行，如果您能理解的话。有些产品为了追求所谓的“合成病毒性传播”而失败了。因为到头来，如果产品本身很糟糕，用户体验不佳，那就完了。就拿Hotmail来说，人们谈论的病毒式标签。我不知道您是否明白我的意思？因为我——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely, at the bottom, yes [inaudible 00:51:34].
turns.zh: 没错，底层逻辑就是这样，对 [00:51:34的模糊音频]。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Well remember, it wasn't just that. It was one of the first webmail things. And webmail was revolutionary because you didn't have to have a POP3 client and lose your email across multiple devices. It solved a lot of really good problems for customers at the time for email. And so when they arrived from the free account, it was like, holy crap, this is amazing. And so let's do that. Uber doesn't have any weird viral traps, but it compresses the workflow of getting a cab so much that it's viral, if that makes sense. In fact, it was this time where Austin kicked them out for and other apps came in and filled the void, and then it came back after the year and just crushed everybody. There was no campaign, it was just viral by itself. So that's what virality is. So then the question is how do you increase it? (00:52:30): Well look, fundamentally build a great product that solves a sharp problem and build it really well. If you do this, this is the bedrock of virality. If you don't do this, there's no viral tactic that will work in a sustained way. It will fizzle. But if you do this, you can lay on synthetic virality strategies for referral, strategies for coming back into the app and creating an account. Remember before Calendly, there was Acuity scheduling, there was other things. The difference was Calendly was so well-made, so simple for schedulers, so respectful of schedulers' time, not just the creator's time that the virality worked. It did not work for others who sucked. Xted AI and other places, they weren't that good. You have to be good to be viral.
turns.zh: 请记住，这不只是一个产品。它是首批网络邮件服务之一，而网络邮件之所以具有革命性，是因为用户无需安装POP3客户端，也无需在不同设备间来回切换查收邮件。这为当时的用户解决了诸多痛点。所以当免费账户涌入时，人们惊呼“天哪，这太棒了”，于是纷纷加入其中。优步（Uber）虽然没有那些奇特的病毒式传播策略，但它极大地简化了叫车流程，这才让它能像病毒般传播开来——如果这能让你明白其中的道理的话。事实上，正是奥斯汀市将优步赶出当地市场后，其他应用涌入填补空白，随后优步在一年后卷土重来，彻底击败所有竞争对手。这并非精心策划的营销活动，而是产品本身的魅力所致。所以关键问题在于如何提升病毒式传播效果？（00:52:30）：说真的，从根本上打造一款能解决核心痛点的优质产品，并精心打磨其体验。如果做到这一点，这就是病毒式传播的基础。若未能达成目标，再多的营销手段也难以持续奏效，最终只能半途而废。但只要做好了基础工作，后续的推荐策略、用户回访策略以及账户创建策略才能真正发挥作用。在Calendly之前，市场上有Acuity Scheduling等同类产品。但Calendly的独特之处在于：其界面设计极为简洁，预约流程对用户友好，充分尊重用户的时间投入——而非只关注创作者的便利性——这才成就了病毒式传播。其他竞品之所以失败，是因为产品体验太差。Xted AI等产品之所以不行，就是因为本身质量不达标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such an important insight, that everyone looks at Calendly like of course you're sharing calendars with everyone, it's going to go viral. That's like what a cool trick. But your point is so interesting that there's previous versions of that, but the product itself wasn't great. The experience wasn't great. It was too complicated, it didn't work, and that's what made it so viral.
turns.zh: 这真是个深刻的洞见。人们总以为Calendly之所以能迅速传播，是因为用户能轻松与他人共享日程表，但你的观点更有趣：市场上早有类似产品，但因产品体验糟糕而失败。Xted AI等竞品之所以不行，就是因为质量不达标。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, there may be several things I think affect virality. But I think that this is the nugget that people need to take away, that is the foundation of bedrock of all of them. Customer support actually affects virality. If you have fanatical customer support, people will love it. Viral tactics like the page that says, oh, get an account, and so on. All these signing documents, Calendly and so on and so forth. Network effects as in Calendly, you have these green dots. If you and a person have, Calendly tells you when you're free, all network effects, really high quality execution, synthetic virality all contribute to net virality. But the fundamental is exactly what we just discussed.
turns.zh: 没错，影响病毒式传播的因素可能有很多。但最核心的关键在于，病毒式传播的基础是产品本身的卓越体验。客户支持对病毒式传播同样重要。优质的客户支持能赢得用户口碑。像“立即注册”等推广页面，以及签署文档等功能。Calendly的绿色点亮效果等网络效应，真正高水平的执行力，以及合成性病毒式传播，都为病毒式传播助力。但根本点在于我们刚刚讨论的核心要素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just got to get it all right. No big deal.
turns.zh: 关键在于把每个环节都做好。没那么难。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Build the best product possible, honestly, if you want to be viral. Slack wasn't even viral, there was no synthetic virality. Slack couldn't even connect to organizations for the longest time. Why? You could be working on the third floor and so on, using Slack on the fourth floor, and you would have no clue. There's no way to share it with them. But what happens when you went to lunch? People are like, "We got Slack and this is amazing." And people on the third floor are like, "Holy shit, when can we get it?" Boom, boom, boom. Great product first is virality.
turns.zh: 如果你想让产品病毒式传播，首先要打造出极致的产品。Slack甚至不具备病毒式传播能力，没有合成性病毒式传播。Slack很长一段时间都无法接入企业系统。为什么？你在三楼工作，四楼的人用Slack，你根本不知道。想和他们分享也无从下手。可午餐时人们发现“我们用了Slack，太棒了”，三楼的人又问“什么时候能用？”轰隆，轰隆，轰隆。产品先行才是病毒式传播的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Seth Godin has this phrase they always come back to, if you want to make your product remarkable, something people want to remark about, and that's basically the core of word of mouth.
turns.zh: 赛斯·高汀（Seth Godin）常提及这样一个观点：如果你想让你的产品引人注目，让人们津津乐道，这基本上就是口碑营销的核心。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yes, yes, yes.
turns.zh: 是的，是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was watching a talk you did on this kind of topic and you had this great phrase that you sort of touched on, but I think it's so good, and I just want to make sure we highlight it, which is that virality is customer augmented marketing.
turns.zh: 我之前看过你关于这个主题的演讲，你提到了一个很棒的观点，但我觉得它太棒了，所以想确保我们能重点强调一下，就是病毒式传播是客户助力的营销。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, I think it is the thing that I started with first. It's when your marketing is essentially done by your customers because what it does, it affords you the ability to spend less on marketing. And you can either uplevel your marketing execution or save money that you can put in the product. Atlassian spends maybe like 10, 20 percentage points less on marketing than the equivalent competitors because it's viral and also because it's network effects at this point as well, say Jira. And so it's customer augmented marketing. Your customers are either forcing other people to adopt it or shaming them into adopting it or FOMOing them into adopting it. So yes, virality is essentially customer oriented marketing, which gives you options.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这就是我最先提到的核心概念。当你的营销主要由客户来完成时，它能为你节省营销成本，让你有更多资金投入产品或提升营销效果。例如，Atlassian在营销上的投入比同类竞争对手低10%到20%，因为Jira等产品具有病毒式传播效应和网络效应。这就是客户助力的营销。你的客户会迫使其他人采用你的产品，或通过羞辱他们、制造紧迫感来促使他们转换。所以没错，病毒式传播本质上是以客户为导向的营销，它为你提供了更多选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that phrase, I'm going to use it now. I have just a few more questions before we get to a very exciting lightning round, and these are kind of random two topics that I wanted to chat on. One is this concept that you call forest time. It's a post you wrote about the importance of forest time. Can you just describe what that is and why it's so important, and then also just how to do this?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个说法了，现在就用起来。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，我还有几个问题想问。其中一个是关于你提到的"森林时间"（Forest Time）的概念。这是你写的一篇关于"森林时间"重要性的文章。能否请你解释一下什么是"森林时间"，它为何如此重要，以及如何践行这一理念？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I operate, I'm an operator right now, meaning that I'm building things, I work for a company. But I also advise and invest, which is different. When I'm advising, I'm looking from above, from outside, I have a bird's eye view and I'm able to say, "You know what? This will work. This won't work. What have you done? Can I look at the results?" And then cycle the advice based on what you're seeing and what I'm seeing. When I'm operating, I'm building a team, I'm hiring, I'm managing all the things, Alina, shout out that hates sometimes. And that's what I'm doing. When you are operating, you have the tug of war. It is so intense that you don't have the attention to have a bird's eye view constantly. (00:57:39): And so forest time is the idea that you make time within your week, within your month to see the forest for the trees. Most of the time when you're operating, you're seeing the tree, which is the problem in front of you. But sometimes you need to see the forest, so you can figure out it as an alternate path, different from the one that you are currently on your campaign. And so it's time to elevate, to get some bird's eye view, to see the entire landscape and see the alternative paths through the current problems that you're escaping. And I think that it has to be very intentional. And intentionality there is, I have published a workflow, a document that helps you make that step to make that elevation. (00:58:25): Like what are the issues? What are alternative ways to solve this potentially that I'm not seeing? Et cetera. And what I try to do is I try to create that forest time for my executive team as well because it's not just me that suffers from this, it's most everybody. In fact, it's most PMs because PMs are so influential that the spoke of the wheel of product creation and product development that we often, it's a sine wave. You are discovering and shaping problems and then you are commanding and captaining execution. And it's endless and they're endless meetings. And so you need to create time for forest time, for elevation. If you don't, you'll become less effective over time. It's just attrition.
turns.zh: 我现在是一名运营者，也就是说，我在负责搭建团队、招聘员工、管理各项事务——阿丽娜（Alina）有时会对此颇有微词。这就是我的日常工作。但我同时也提供咨询和投资服务，这两者有所不同。作为顾问，我需要从宏观视角审视问题：我会站在局外审视全局，说：“这个方案可行，这个方案行不通。你做了什么？能让我看看结果吗？”然后根据实际情况调整建议。作为运营者，我需要亲力亲为，组建团队、招聘人员、处理各种事务——阿丽娜有时会对此颇有微词。这就是我的日常工作。在运营阶段，压力重重，根本无暇顾及宏观视角。（00:57:39）所以“森林时间”指的是在每周或每月中抽出时间跳出日常琐事，审视大局。多数时候，身处运营岗位的我们只关注眼前的树木，也就是眼前的问题。但有时我们需要退后一步，审视整个森林，寻找突破现有困境的替代路径。这就需要提升视野，跳出固有思维模式。我为此专门编写了一份工作流程文档，帮助团队成员实现这种思维转变。（00:58:25）比如：问题出在哪里？有没有可能采用我们尚未考虑到的解决方案？等等。我还努力为我的管理团队创造这种“森林时间”，因为这不仅是我个人的困扰，也是大多数人的共性问题。事实上，大多数产品经理都深受其害，因为产品经理是产品创造和开发的核心力量，通常处于产品生命周期的波峰与波谷之间：先是发现并塑造问题，接着指挥执行。这是一个无穷无尽的循环，会议永无止境。因此，我们需要为提升视野留出时间。如果不这样做，效率迟早会被消磨殆尽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then just to make it even more concrete for people, what are examples of forest time? Is it taking time off? Is it advising on the side? Is it-
turns.zh: 再具体说说什么是“森林时间”？是休假吗？是兼职咨询吗？还是——

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: It is taking a day off at the end of a month, a full day or two days. And instead of just playing golf, although that's fine, it is doing a workflow, worksheet to survey the forest specifically. And sometimes managers are like, "Wait, you're giving people a day off when they should be working harder and harder?" And I think it's completely worth it. It's not about working harder, it's working smarter. It's about seeing more options than you see. And so I'm very happy to give that time to product managers, to product executives or design executives or engineering executives. (01:00:01): Because I think that if they do it properly, then we'll have better execution in the long run. Let's put it this way, in product development, we aim for maybe like 10% of the time and then we execute and build for the other side. It's not just, there's more stuff we do. If your aim is off, then you are spending one, $2 million incorrectly of people's time. And so forest time should improve your aim. That's the entire point, because your aim is a precursor to a huge amount of investment. And so I think it's well worth it.
turns.zh: 就是在月底抽出一天或两天完整的休息时间。不是去打高尔夫（虽然打高尔夫也不错），而是通过工作流程和工作表，专门审视大局。有时候管理者会问：“等等，你们给人放一天假，他们不是应该更拼命工作吗？”我觉得这完全值得。重点不在于加班，而在于更高效地工作。关键在于开拓更多视野。因此，我很乐意为产品经理、产品高管、设计高管或工程高管提供这种时间。（01:00:01）因为我相信，如果他们能合理利用这段时间，长期来看我们的执行效率会更高。打个比方，在产品开发中，我们可能只投入10%的时间用于构思，然后投入90%的时间去执行。如果构思偏差，就意味着浪费了两百万美元的人力成本。因此，“森林时间”应该能帮助我们校准目标。这才是核心意义所在，因为目标是后续大量投入的先决条件。所以我认为这非常值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. So specifically what you do with your team is once a month, you give them a day to do this kind of worksheet that you put together?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。具体来说，你每月一次让团队成员花一天时间完成你整理的这类工作表吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then that worksheet is in this post that you wrote, that you point to. Is that right?
turns.zh: 然后这个工作表就在你写的这篇帖子里，你提到的那个，对吧？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Correct, correct.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, great. This is very practical advice. I love it. Okay, one last question before a very exciting lightning round. You worked at Bridgewater Associates, which I didn't know until I started digging into your past. That sounds creepy. And Bridgewater Associates famous for what? Ray Dalio's hedge fund, author of Principals and all these other incredible books, and it's a very unique working environment. So I just wanted to ask about your experience there, specifically one of the craziest things there is just this thing called dots I think it's called, where people just call out mistakes that people make at the company and it's public. Is that how it actually was? Any memories of that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，很棒。这真是非常实用的建议。我很喜欢。在开始深入了解你的过往经历之前，我还不知道你曾在桥水基金工作。这听起来有点吓人。桥水基金以什么闻名呢？雷·达利奥的对冲基金，他写了《原则》等多本精彩著作，而且那里的工作环境非常独特。所以我想问问你在那里的经历，特别是他们那套“点评文化”——就是公开指责公司里别人的错误。这是真实存在的吗？你对此有什么记忆吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I was a senior management, what's called an SMA, which is the management layer right under Ray's team. And we were the priests of the Church of Bridgewater. Bridgewater did things like record, this is public knowledge, I'm not saying anything-
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我当时是高级管理层，简称SMA，属于雷的团队下方的一个管理层。我们被称为桥水基金的“牧师”。桥水基金有一些做法，比如记录员工的错误行为，这都是公开的，不是我乱说——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, he writes about-
turns.zh: 是的，雷在书里写过——

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: ... before every meeting. Eventually we created a dot collector, which allows you to rate people in real time. So I'm just having a conversation with you and before the meeting closes, in front of each other, I pull up my laptop and I rate you and rate the interaction. And in theory, the idea is that if you constantly rate people across hundreds of interactions, then you build a picture of them that is fairly accurate, statistically accurate, that will transcend maybe emotional relationship as wisdom of the crowd idea. So that's a theory. In practice, it is emotionally exhausting. And like you said, the little creepy, even the recording. (01:02:38): So I think there were things about Bridgewater that I understood intellectually in terms of the purpose that Ray had designed, but didn't quite work. It's like the way I think about this is the theory of the principles are really good. The practice and the execution can be quite off and not very human or not very empathetic. But I will say this, Bridgewater taught me things that I don't think any other organization in the world thought taught me. One example is Bridgewater thinks of people in three dimensions, their skills, their attributes, and their values. Most organizations think about people in terms of just their skills. But it makes sense that people have attributes and values, that people are timid, people are bold, people like to jump in, people like to stand back. (01:03:38): All these other things, we think about personality and proclivity. Bridgewater tries to establish and measure them and also tries to write job descriptions that say, this is the kind of attributes we're looking for, not just the skills we're looking for. And then of course values. Are you a thief or are you a principled? And so on and so forth. Now that idea of looking at talent or people in general, both in your professional life and in your personal life, is a huge addition to me as a professional from Bridgewater. So I'm saying that there were things I didn't enjoy about Bridgewater, but things that I learned that I've learned nowhere else as well.
turns.zh: 每次会议前，我们都会这样做。最终，我们开发了一个“点数收集器”，能让大家实时给同事打分。比如，我现在正在和你们交流，会议结束前，我们会当面拿出笔记本电脑，互相打分。从理论上讲，如果你能在数百次互动中持续评估他人，就能构建出相当准确、具有统计意义的画像，这种画像或许能超越情感关系，形成所谓的“群体智慧”。但在实践中，这实在令人心力交瘁。正如你所说，甚至连录音功能都让人觉得有点毛骨悚然。（01:02:38）：所以，我对桥水公司的理解是，雷·达里奥设计的目标理念本质上是好的，但执行效果却不尽如人意。比如，我认为他们的原则理论很棒，但实际操作和执行却存在偏差，缺乏人性化和同理心。但我要说的是，桥水教会了我一些其他组织从未传授过的理念。比如，桥水用三维视角看待人才——技能、特质和价值观。大多数公司只关注技能，但桥水认为人有特质和价值观，比如胆小、勇敢、积极参与、保持观望等。我们关注个性和倾向性，努力量化这些特质，并编写职位描述时强调所需的价值观，而不仅仅是技能。还有价值观部分，比如判断一个人是小偷还是有原则的人等等。现在，无论是职场还是个人生活中，用这种方式审视人才的能力，都是我在桥水获得的宝贵收获。当然，桥水也有让我不适的地方，但从专业角度来看，这些收获是无与伦比的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you take that to what you do today? Thinking of people in those three different ways and-
turns.zh: 你有没有把这些理念应用到现在的工作中？用这三种不同的视角看待人才——

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: 100%. in my professional life, in my personal life, when I interview people, I am cognizant of those three things and I try to extract those three things, because I think it improves your success. Famously, all the weird skill-based interviewing at Google was only 50/50 predictive. And the reason is Google did not consider the other two things, I believe. Bridgewater was willing to endure 80% attrition to arrive at the best people. Now I don't think it works for them because some of their system was not empathetic of humans, like expecting humans to be computers. But I thought that was a very important insight.
turns.zh: 百分之百正确。在职场和个人生活中，面试时我都会关注这三个维度，并努力挖掘它们，因为我相信这能提升成功率。众所周知，谷歌那些奇怪的基于技能的面试预测准确率只有50%。这是因为谷歌没有考虑其他两个维度。我认为桥水愿意承受80%的离职率，只为招到最优秀的人才。不过我觉得他们的系统对人类不够友好，比如期望人像计算机一样运作。但我认为这是一个非常重要的洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Oji, is there anything else that you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Oji，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: In the history of product development, we have basically started to create abstraction to guide our work versus the Wild, Wild West. So the engineers came up with agile and peer programming and all these things. The designers have come up with design thinking, design sprints, and combined with research to talk about how to do discovery of various complexity. And the question is the product abstractions, because there's code, there's product in this business. So the product and business layer, what is our abstraction? What is our crucible for organizing our work? (01:05:52): We don't even have one. We don't have a name for it. And so the idea of a part system is that there's an abstraction above agile and design thinking that we have to pay attention to build solid organizations and to execute well at the product and the business layer. This is a co-creative framework with me and Ezinne. And the idea here is how do you construct a good product system? And literally, you could boil it down into a checklist of the systems you need to build a really good cohesive R and D organization. So I think that's the tee up. I'm going to have to leave you thirsty because someone else is probably going to go deep into it.
turns.zh: 在产品开发史上，我们基本上开始创建抽象概念来指导我们的工作，而非任由其自由发展。因此，工程师们提出了敏捷开发和对等编程等方法；设计师们则开发了设计思维、设计冲刺等理念，并结合研究来探讨如何探索各种复杂问题的解决方案。关键在于产品抽象层——毕竟在这个行业中，既有代码，也有产品。因此，产品与业务层的抽象概念是什么？我们组织工作的核心框架是什么？（01:05:52）：我们甚至没有一个统一的框架。我们甚至没有一个专有名词来定义它。那么，零部件系统这个概念是什么？它是敏捷开发和设计思维之上的一个抽象层级，我们必须关注它，以构建稳固的组织，并在产品和业务层面高效执行。这是我和Ezinne共同开发的协作框架。其核心在于如何构建一个优秀的产品系统。简而言之，你可以将其归纳为构建一个真正高效的研发组织所需的系统清单。接下来就交给你们去深入探讨了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And that's your wife that you mentioned who you are co-creating this framework with and who we're going to have on the podcast in the future.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到与你共同开发这个框架的妻子，我们未来还会邀请她上播客。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is it like being married to another product leader? Would you recommend?
turns.zh: 与另一位产品负责人结婚是什么感觉？你会推荐吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: 100%, you can have really productive conversations and you can redesign other company's applications in one conversation in the evening.
turns.zh: 百分之百推荐。你们可以进行非常高效的对话，甚至在晚上的一次谈话中就重新设计其他公司的应用程序。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well, that was almost the lightning round question, but I moved it up earlier. And so with that we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，那差不多到了闪电问答环节了。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, I'm ready. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 是的，我准备好了。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. Let's do it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。开始吧。你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: There's one business book that I recommend, I think it's called The Halo Effect. It's basically a book that lets you call on all these business books that tell you all kinds of stupid shit. It is how to deconstruct what is important in a business and self-help book and what is not important and what is just circumstantial storytelling with random facts and form-fitting evidence. It's called The Halo Effect. Read it. Why do you need to read it? Because garbage in, garbage Out. (01:07:45): People were amazed at the Outlier Effect, Malcolm Gladwell, and then people have been tearing it down for 15 years now. But everyone ingested it and thought it was the most important thing. But how do you know what's important to take away from them and what's not? The Halo Effect will help you. And then the other thing is, I read for pleasure because I read a lot for work. And so science fiction is the thing. There's lots to recommend, but I would say that people should either read Dune, Frank Herbert or Foundation by Asimov. If you haven't read those two things and you're a science fiction person, you really should. The world building is incredible. I understand Tolkien and fantasy, but the science fiction side of it is those two books.
turns.zh: 有一本商业书籍我推荐，叫《光环效应》。这本书能让你质疑所有那些告诉你各种无稽之谈的商业书籍。它教你如何解构商业和自助书籍中真正重要的内容，以及那些只是附带故事、随意拼凑证据的部分。就叫《光环效应》。去读吧。为什么要读？因为输入什么，就会输出什么。（01:07:45）：人们对《异类效应》惊叹不已，马尔科姆·格拉德威尔的作品也曾广受追捧，但15年来，人们一直在批判它。但每个人都接受了这些观点，认为它们至关重要。但你如何判断哪些是真正值得借鉴的，哪些只是附带的故事和随意拼凑的证据？《光环效应》会帮你分辨。另外，我因为工作需要大量阅读，所以也为了乐趣而阅读。科幻小说是我的最爱。有很多推荐，但我建议大家读弗兰克·赫伯特的《沙丘》或阿西莫夫的《基地》。如果你没读过这两部作品，又是科幻爱好者，那真是太遗憾了。其中的世界观构建令人惊叹。我理解托尔金和奇幻作品，但科幻领域的这两部作品堪称典范。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's also a TV series of Foundation now, which I can say recommend absolutely. But it's a beautiful show.
turns.zh: 如今《基地》也拍成电视剧了，这部剧我绝对推荐。但它真是一部美轮美奂的作品。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Yeah, no. I haven't watched Foundation yet. I just felt super weird watching it after reading it. And I could only make it through three quarters of Dune. Well one, but I will make it through them. I don't expect them... The books are glorious. If you love prose, the books are, man, crazy. But I will get through them eventually.
turns.zh: 是啊，不用说。我还没看过《基地》。不过读完原著后再看剧，感觉怪怪的。而《沙丘》我只看完了四分之三。好吧，也许有一天能看完。但我不抱太大希望……原著太棒了。如果你喜欢散文，那这套书简直是狂暴的存在。不过我总会看完它们的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've not actually read Dune, but the movie was incredible. I played the video game Dune where you're just mining spice all day and it's just stuck in my brain forever. Okay, next question. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 我其实没读过《沙丘》，但那部电影太棒了。我玩过《沙丘》游戏，就是每天挖矿开采香料的，那游戏画面至今让我念念不忘。好吧，下一个问题。你面试候选人时，最喜欢问的两个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I try to ask two. I feel like it's going to give people a cheat sheet when I interview them. But I try to ask two questions. So I'm not a person who does favorites, so it's hard for me to pick favorites. But I ask people to introduce themselves and I think it tells me a lot about them, how they tell about themselves, what they say about themselves and the content of it. I ask people about the things they think they're truly great at and then I ask people the things they think they need to learn. The latter too is about their professional skill, their craft. I think it tells me a lot about how they communicate, it tells me a lot about how thoughtful they are. It tells me a lot about what they're proud of and what they lead into. And those kinds of things are very important to me.
turns.zh: 我尽量问两个。我觉得如果每次面试都问一样的问题，会让候选人觉得有标准答案。不过我还是会问两个问题。一个是自我介绍，这能让我了解他们，观察他们的表达方式和内容。另一个是让他们说出自己最擅长的事和需要提升的技能。这既能考察他们的专业能力，也能观察他们的沟通和思考方式。这些细节对我很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I have been optimizing my workspace a lot. So I'm on a kick right now where I use Windows. I was in the Windows PM and I still have my Windows box. But a lot of people, we use Mac at work and I've used Mac for the last few years. So even though I switched between them, I've spent a lot more time on Mac and my Windows experience is completely optimized. It is perfect. But Mac, I'm like the Windowing sucks, there's all these gaps I see. So I've been trying to figure out how to dial in my Mac experience. (01:10:49): I hate the activity monitor, sucks. What's a replacement? The sound. It doesn't support sound through HDMI or sound through... I don't know, just some weird setup. So I've been optimizing that. One particular product that I like in the context of that is Unlocks. It's one man product that allows me to just look at my phone and log into my Mac when I walk up and then locks it when I walk away. And it'll actually detect my proximity. So it'll start the login process while I get close. I think that's incredible and I feel like it improves my productivity.
turns.zh: 我最近一直在优化我的工作环境。现在我痴迷于Windows系统。我曾在Windows项目组工作，现在还留着那台Windows电脑。但很多人工作用Mac，我自己过去几年也一直用Mac。所以尽管我在这两者间切换过，但用Mac的时间更多，现在Windows体验已经完美了。但Mac系统……我觉得窗口管理太糟糕了，到处都是漏洞。所以我一直在优化Mac体验。（01:10:49）：我讨厌活动监视器，太烂了。有什么替代品吗？还有声音问题，HDMI接口不支持声音输出……我也不知道，设置太奇怪了。所以我一直在优化这部分。其中一个特别喜欢的工具是Unlocks。这是个单人开发的软件，让我走近电脑就能自动登录，离开时自动锁屏。它能检测到我的位置变化。登录过程会在我靠近时自动启动。我觉得这太棒了，大大提高了我的工作效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. Sounds like a lot of haterade for Macs over here.
turns.zh: 真酷。听起来你对Mac电脑挺有意见的。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Well, for someone who uses it a lot, no, I think pros and cons. I'm no longer paid by Microsoft, so there are things I don't like. But there are also things that the Mac isn't perfect either.
turns.zh: 嗯，作为常用用户，我觉得优缺点都有。微软不再给我发工资了，所以有些地方我不喜欢。但Mac系统也有不完美的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, indeed. What is a favorite life motto that you repeat to yourself or share with other people, either in work or in life that you find valuable?
turns.zh: 是啊，很有道理。你有没有什么特别珍视的人生格言，既能激励自己，又能与他人分享，无论是在工作中还是生活中？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I've taken to saying that there's more knowledge outside my head than inside it. And this is a plea for curiosity. I have three main things that are my North Star personally. Obviously when I say personally, I mean everything professionally. Which is originality, curiosity, and wisdom. And so this thing about there's more knowledge outside my head than inside my head is a plea for curiosity, it's a plea for skepticism. It's a plea to be humble about what you know, no matter how old you are, about the world around you, and always be listening for more. Even when you know something, let other people speak because they might add 10% more to the 90% you know. And so being an active listener is very important.
turns.zh: 我常说，我的脑袋里装着的知识远不及脑袋外面的多。说这话，是在呼吁保持好奇心。我个人认为，对我而言，职业生涯中最重要的三个核心价值观是：原创力、好奇心和智慧。所以，当我说"脑袋外面的知识比脑袋里的多"时，其实是在呼吁保持好奇心，呼吁保持怀疑精神。呼吁谦逊地认识自己所知，认识周遭的世界，时刻保持倾听的姿态。即便你已经掌握了某些知识，也要让别人发声——因为他们能为你已知的90%知识再添上10%的价值。积极倾听至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. Last question, you are from Nigeria. What is a Nigerian food that you think people need to find and get ASAP?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个问题，你来自尼日利亚。有什么尼日利亚美食是你觉得人们应该尽快去寻找尝试的？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I'll recommend two, depending on how familiar you are. So if you've never had fried plantain with beef stew-
turns.zh: 我会推荐两种，取决于你对它们的熟悉程度。如果你从未品尝过炸木薯搭配炖牛肉——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, that sounds great.
turns.zh: 天哪，听起来太棒了。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: ... then you should stop what you're doing, stop work, whatever you're doing, find your next Nigerian friend and go get some, okay? This is the food that most Nigerians will basically trade years of life to have access to, okay. So that's what I would say. And then the second thing is if you want to be in the in club in Nija, as we call it, you got to try pepper soup.
turns.zh: ……那你得停下手头的事，停下工作，停下任何正在做的事，找个尼日利亚朋友去尝尝，好吗？这道美食是大多数尼日利亚人愿意为之付出多年光阴也要品尝到的，明白吗？所以我会这么推荐。第二道美食是，如果你想加入我们所谓的"尼日利亚圈子"，就得尝尝辣椒汤。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Pepper soup.
turns.zh: 辣椒汤。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: Now, if you all are not into spicy stuff, I'm sorry, the door is close to you. But pepper soup is really... And it is amazing. It'll make you sweat, but it's delicious and you should give it a shot.
turns.zh: 现在，如果你们不喜欢辣的东西，那很遗憾，你们不符合条件。但辣椒汤真的……太棒了。它会让你出汗，但味道绝佳，你应该试试看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oji, I think we've solved many people's sharp problems. I really appreciate you making time being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: oji，我觉得我们已经解决了很多人急切想知道的问题。非常感谢你抽空来这里。最后两个问题。读者如果想联系你，可以在哪里找到你？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: I publish on Substack when I have time, you should check it out. It's usually all about things that are beneath the surface. What's behind the thing. I believe that's how you'll find it. I'm on Twitter as well, so you can follow me because I will talk about products. How you can be useful to me is go follow me on Twitter, sign up for updates on the book. If you do, I will draw from that audience to help name the book, to help design the cover for the book. The book is intended to have a freemium because I want this book to be available to people in Africa and India, across the world. So there'll be a free version of it and there'll be premium versions with more tools, more help, and maybe even interviews with luminaries that you care and love as well. And so hopefully that will fund the free side of it as well. So come in, become part of the party, maybe join a pre-read, an early draft read. That is the best way you can help. So this is a call to all PMs and people of goodwill.
turns.zh: 我有空的时候会在Substack上发文，你可以去看看。内容通常都是深层探讨的，探究事物背后的真相。我相信这才是找到真相的途径。我也在Twitter上，你可以关注我，因为我会谈论产品。听众如何能为我提供帮助，就是去Twitter上关注我，订阅新书更新。如果你这么做了，我会从这些读者中抽取人来为书命名，设计书的封面。本书计划采用免费增值模式，因为我想让非洲、印度以及全球各地的人都能读到这本书。所以会有免费版本，也会有付费版本，提供更多工具、更多帮助，甚至可能采访你所关心的和喜爱的杰出人物。希望这样能为免费版本提供资金支持。所以快来加入吧，或许参与预读、早期草稿阅读。这是你们能提供最大帮助的方式。所以这是向所有产品经理和善意之人的呼吁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What a great answer to that question. I'm going to go get some pepper soup and some plantain beef meals. Thank you so much for being here, and I'm going to go get some food.
turns.zh: 太棒了。对这个问题的回答真是精彩绝伦。我要去吃些辣椒汤和炸木薯牛肉餐了。非常感谢你来这里，我要去吃点东西了。

turns.speaker: Oji Udezue
turns.en: All right. Thank you, Lenny. It was super enjoyable and love hanging out and God speed.
turns.zh: 好的。谢谢你，Lenny。今天非常愉快，很高兴能相聚，祝你一帆风顺。
